standard.title: Language signals social roles
standard.description: Understand that language is selected for social contexts and that it helps to signal social roles and relationships
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore language used to develop relationships in formal and informal situations (AC9E4LA01). They have not yet examined how language choices actively signal social roles and relationships, or considered cultural protocols and how silence/formality norms vary across communities.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how specific language choices signal social roles and relationships in context, identify how formality registers shift across situations, and describe how communication norms and protocols differ across cultural contexts including those of First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Register and social context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that language varies in formality according to the social context, and name examples of formal and informal language in familiar situations.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of language choices that shift between a formal and informal version of the same communication (e.g. 'Could you please pass the report?' vs 'Can you grab that?').
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain how language formality signals context across a range of situations: classroom, playground, formal presentation, adult conversation. Match language choices to context purpose and relationships involved.
wider: Explore how digital communication contexts (texting, email, social media) generate their own register norms, and how these sit on a formal–informal continuum
Examine transcripts or scripts from different social situations and sort language choices onto a formality spectrum, justifying placements
nodes.hinge_reason: Register as a context-sensitive continuum is foundational to Node 2's analysis of role-signalling and Node 4's multi-criteria language selection framework. Students who treat formality as binary (on/off) rather than as a contextually calibrated spectrum will be unable to reason about how fine-grained language choices signal specific roles and relationships in Node 2.

response_modes.reason: Students often treat formality as binary (formal/informal) rather than as a spectrum that shifts continuously with context. Encountering diverse situations — school, sport, family, online — helps students see that register is contextually calibrated, not switched on or off.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two ways language choices (vocabulary, sentence structure, tone) differ between formal and informal contexts.
Explains why a specific language choice is appropriate or inappropriate for a given social situation.

nodes.label: Language signals roles and relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how particular language choices signal roles (e.g. chairperson, speaker, expert) and the relationships between participants in an interaction.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how language choices in a structured context (e.g. a classroom debate or formal discussion) signal who holds which role, and explain what those choices communicate about the relationship between participants.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse examples from debate, formal discussion, and workplace contexts to explain how language signals authority, deference, peer equality, or expertise. Explain the consequences of role-mismatched language choices.
wider: Compare how language signals roles in formal Australian institutional contexts (parliament, courtroom, formal ceremony) versus informal peer contexts, discussing what makes the role-signalling legible

Examine how roles and relationships are signalled in texts written by First Nations Australian authors, identifying language choices that reflect cultural protocols around seniority, kinship or ceremony
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 4's integration task requires students to apply criteria for language selection that explicitly include roles and relationships. Students who cannot explain how language choices signal roles — not just identify that formality shifts — will be unable to account for the roles-and-relationships criterion in Node 4's multi-criteria analysis.

response_modes.reason: The connection between a specific language choice and the role it signals is not always transparent to students. A reasoning scaffold — 'what role does this language position the speaker in, and how does the listener know?' — helps students develop the analytical move needed to explain rather than just identify.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Role-signalling through language is genuinely rich across formal/informal, institutional/cultural, and digital/face-to-face contexts. Advancing students can investigate how the same sentence can signal different roles in different contexts, and examine how First Nations Australian communication protocols encode relational knowledge — providing genuine depth without exceeding year band.
success_criteria: Identifies a specific language choice and explains which role it signals and for whom.
Explains how the relationship between participants shapes the language choice made (not just identifies the relationship).

nodes.label: Cultural variation in communication norms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how communication norms — including degrees of formality, periods of silence, and cultural protocols — differ across cultures, including First Nations Australian practices.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one way that communication norms differ between cultural contexts, and explain what those differences signal about social relationships or values in that context.
nodes.typical_width: Describe how communication norms vary across cultural contexts examined in class, including aspects such as silence, turn-taking, degrees of formality, and directness. Explain that these differences reflect different cultural understandings of respectful interaction, not deficits.
wider: Research and describe specific communication protocols of a First Nations Australian community, explaining the social or relational meaning those protocols carry
Compare responses to common requests across cultural contexts studied, identifying how the same communicative intent is expressed differently and what values underpin those differences

response_modes.reason: Students commonly interpret unfamiliar communication norms through a deficit lens ('why don't they just say it directly?'). Encountering multiple cultural communication contexts — including silence as meaningful, indirect as respectful, formal as relational — helps students understand variation as culturally purposeful rather than as error.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australian communication protocols offer genuinely rich content at this node — protocols around kinship, ceremony, and elder speech encode social roles through language in ways that extend students' understanding of how language signals relationships. This is pedagogically rich and within year band scope.
success_criteria: Describes at least one communication norm from a cultural context different from their own and explains what social meaning it carries.
Avoids framing cultural communication differences as incorrect or inferior — explains differences as purposeful within their context.

nodes.label: Selecting language for context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain and apply criteria for selecting language appropriate to a social context, accounting for purpose, roles, relationships and cultural norms.
nodes.minimum_width: For a given social situation, identify the key contextual factors (purpose, roles, relationships, cultural norms) and explain how those factors would inform specific language choices.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse and explain language choices across several contrasting social contexts, accounting for purpose, roles, relationships and cultural context. Apply these criteria to evaluate the appropriateness of language choices in sample texts or interactions.
wider: Examine how mismatches between language choice and social context create meaning effects (e.g. humour, irony, social friction, power assertion), and explain what those effects reveal about the social norms in play
Investigate how language in formal roles changes across time periods (e.g. parliamentary language, legal language) and discuss what those changes indicate about shifting social relationships

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate register knowledge (node 1), role-signalling (node 2), and cultural variation (node 3) into a unified analytical framework for language selection. The integration — applying multiple criteria simultaneously to evaluate a language choice — is the learning at this node.

success_criteria: Identifies at least three contextual factors that inform language selection and applies them to explain a specific language choice.
Evaluates a language choice in a sample text or interaction as appropriate or inappropriate to context, with reference to purpose, roles, and relationships.
